Reconcile an opening balance and its movements to the closing balance

Source: R/check_movement.R
check_movement.Rd

Equity, fixed assets, provisions: an annual report is full of schedules that start from last year's figure, add and subtract during the year, and end at this year's. This checks that each one arrives where it says it does.

Usage

check_movement(
  x,
  statement = NULL,
  period = NULL,
  assume_nil = FALSE,
  by = NULL,
  tol = 1
)

Arguments

x

A tibble from add_taxonomy().

statement

Restrict to these statements. NULL (default) checks every presentation group that has the shape of a schedule – see the section below on what that includes.

period

The filing's declared accounting period, from xbrl_period(). Optional, and worth passing: it settles which year the schedule covers and which instant is its opening balance, where without it both are inferred from the movements' own dates.

assume_nil

Read a single absent balance as zero. See the section below; the result marks every schedule this applies to.

by

Columns identifying one schedule beyond its own group and dimension. Defaults to "basis"; add the company identifier for a panel.

tol

Absolute tolerance in the reporting currency. Default 1.

Value

A tibble with one row per schedule: the by columns, group (the presentation code the schedule sits under), dimension and member where the schedule is broken down, opening, closing, n_movements, n_zero (movements reported as nil, which are excluded from the search because they say nothing about their own sign), movements (whether they were tagged at this level or summed over the classes below it), balances (whether both were reported or one was assumed nil), and status from find_signs().

Why nothing else catches this

Every other check in the package compares like with like. check_statement() compares instants to instants, check_cascade() compares durations to durations, and neither touches the identity that binds them:

opening (instant) + movements (duration) = closing (instant)

That identity is where a schedule can be wrong while every other figure in the filing is right – and it is the only place a company states its investment for the year, which is the figure national accounts want.

The signs are the filer's

A schedule arrives without a usable sign convention. DisposalsOf... is reported positive and must be subtracted; the reversal of depreciation on those same disposals is reported negative and must be added, in the same note. So the movements are handed to find_signs() with the closing balance as the total and the opening balance pinned positive – the identity decides the signs, and a schedule that admits no unique assignment is reported as such rather than guessed at.

Shape is not intent

Nothing in the Danish taxonomy marks a presentation group as a roll-forward, so this recognises one by its shape: a single balance reported at both ends of the period, with movements over that period beside it. Two kinds of group have that shape without the meaning.

A five-year summary (KeyFiguresAndFinancialRatios) sets assets, equity, capital and provisions side by side at two dates each; nothing says which of them the profit in the same group is supposed to explain. Groups holding more than one balance are therefore skipped outright.

A disclosure note (DisclosureOfRelatedParties) quotes equity and profit as context, and that pair is the shape of a schedule – but the note omits every other movement, so the identity cannot close and reports a failure that says nothing about the filing. Shape alone cannot tell it from a real equity statement. Pass statement to scope the check where a schedule is actually meant: StatementOfChangesInEquity and the asset notes.

A balance that is simply blank

By default a schedule is checked only where the balance is reported at both dates. That is the strict reading, and it is often too strict: an asset class that started or ended at nothing is routinely left blank rather than tagged as nil.

assume_nil = TRUE reads one absent balance as zero – one, never both, since a schedule missing both ends is not a schedule. The result says so in balances, because an assumed nil must not travel as a reported one.

What it will not do is infer the opening balance from the identity itself. That would make the check confirm its own assumption, and every schedule would reconcile.

A group holding two elements that each appear at both dates is not one schedule and is skipped whatever this is set to.

See also

find_signs(), which resolves the signs, and check_breakdown(), which checks the same schedules across a dimension rather than through time.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")
m <- check_movement(x)

# the schedules that do not arrive where they say
m[m$status != "unique", ]
} # }
